And castration was strictly forbidden by the church as an act, but they had no compunction about employing the castrati to sing this music. And that made the castrati sort of these featured and fascinating artists for the public, and that happened to coincide with the inception of opera as an art form. And, therefore, these composers started writing all these lead roles for castrated men. And they became the rock stars of their era - the highest-paid singers and these creatures of fascination, and gruesome fascination in a way. But also, it's fascinating to read the doctors' reports about castrati.
GROSS: ...Able to read the doctors' reports?

COSTANZO: Yes. There's a few doctors' reports. You know, it - because it was forbidden by the church, all the castration had to happen behind closed doors, sometimes in the back of barbershops. And this was all forbidden, and so every mother would have to come up with an excuse. A popular one was, my son was bitten by a wild boar. And so it was all a kind of ruse.

And I thought, why are they calling me? You know? And I saw that Plant Man had this little catchphrase in the commercial - no prob, Girl. And I realized that - I imagine the producers thought, oh, let's get an opera singer - and a gay one - who would say something like no prob, Girl, and they Googled gay opera singer and there I was, and they called me and said, will you do it?

So when I got to the studio to record the little jingle for this commercial, they had me singing in what was kind of a tenor range, and I said, well, don't you want me to sing up in the countertenor range? And they said, what's that? And so I sang a note for them, and they said, wow. You're like the Mariah Carey of opera. And I thought that was so funny. And subsequently, I donned a potted plant suit to film the commercial and sang along to that soundtrack. And then Purple launched, and I believe it was Tucker Carlson who - the commentator on Fox News at the time who said, you know, this was about, you know, being woke and all of these things that we shouldn't be doing in a major company like Mars, the candy company - shouldn't be, you know, putting that kind of stuff out. I don't even know what it was all about to be truthful, but it sunk Purple, the purple M&M, and, in fact, it was a prob, Girl.
GROSS: (Laughter) What was it like for you to momentarily be a Tucker Carlson talking point?

COSTANZO: (Laughter) I think that's the height of my career, for sure. You know, if I can enter the zeitgeist with an operatic voice, then I've really reached new heights. You know, opera can feel so distant from what culture is doing sometimes, and my whole mission in life is to bring it closer to everybody. And Tucker Carlson helped me out with that.
COSTANZO: (Laughter) I'd like to hear his countertenor if he's willing.

GROSS: (Laughter) So in addition to being an opera singer, you are the general director and president of the company Opera Philadelphia. And that company here in Philly, where I live, is known for really opening the door to younger people who don't know opera but are curious enough to try it out if you make it accessible in an interesting way. And in order to do that, like, you've produced operas in unusual spaces, you've advertised in unusual places, you've lowered the tickets, you could get tickets for as low as $11. Is that still true?
COSTANZO: Yeah. Now every ticket for every show for the entire season is $11 or pick your price.
GROSS: And - this is innovative - you've advertised on Grindr. And that's, like, the gay dating app. Explain why.

COSTANZO: Yeah, well, you know, when I took over Opera Philadelphia, I was so excited 'cause it was a really innovative company already making great art. But it was in a difficult moment. There was a huge cash crisis. There was debt, and we were getting ready to open a really big opera. So basically, I had 12 weeks to raise $4 million or we were going to go bankrupt. And on top of all of that, we'd only sold about 30% of the tickets for the season that was about to start, and I thought, gosh, you know, we have to change something. And I began to think about what the barriers are for Opera. And I think the biggest barrier is perception. You know, people think that it is elite and in the way the institutions purvey it, sometimes it is. And so I thought, how can we change that perception and also make it fun and make it accessible to people?

And we made every ticket for every seat $11. And within three weeks, our entire season was sold out. We were, I think, the only opera company in America with a sold-out season before it even started. And what we saw is this incredible, you know, information about our demographics - 69% first-time ticket buyers, 67% people under 45. And, you know, it was astonishing to stand in the lobby of that opera house and just see people flood in from all over the country from every ZIP code in Philadelphia and people who had never been to the opera. So I started to think about how we could change the perception and get more people there. And so, first, I took ads out on trash cans. In Philadelphia, there are these big belly trash cans, and most of them have ads up that are like, you know, 1-800-INJURY for a lawyer or something.

COSTANZO: And they'll stay up for a year, you know, and get all graffiti and everything. And I thought, well - you know, an orchestra member said, why don't you get one of those? You'll get a lot of bang for your buck. And she was right. I went and I found that for $5,000, I could buy all these trash cans and put my ads on them, and I'd buy a month of ads, and they would stay up for a year. So it started, you know, from a place of economy. And then I also realized that, what better place than a trash can to encounter the idea of opera, right? It makes it totally non-elitist. And from there, we're experimenting with all kinds of things, including the gay dating app Grindr not only to sell the tickets, but it's also about changing people's perception. What makes opera feel like it could be a fun night out? I mean, opera's about all kinds of crazy, wild things. But it's not this serious, buttoned-up art form. And so I want to make people feel that. And I hope that it changed people's perception. And on the economics front, I found out that you can reach 500,000 people on Grindr for about an $1,000 ad buy, so it's a really good place to reach a lot of people.
GROSS: Well, Anthony, it's been great to talk with you again. I'm so glad we did this.
COSTANZO: Terry, what a great pleasure and honor to talk to you again. Thank you for having me.

GROSS: Anthony Roth Costanzo's new memoir and companion album are called "Countertenor." He's the general director and president of Opera Philadelphia and artistic director of Carnegie Hall's Song Studio.
